papers.title: Continuous karyotypic and cryptic structural fluctuations drive acral melanoma evolution
papers.abstract: Reliable chromosome segregation during mitosis is essential for high-fidelity mammalian cell division. Even human cancers burdened by whole genome duplication and aneuploidy generally retain sufficiently stable segregation to produce clonal populations of progeny. Cancer genomes are accordingly understood to evolve in punctuated bursts, in which catastrophic rearrangement is followed by clonal expansion of a stabilized karyotype. However, bulk genomic sequencing, the workhorse of cancer genetics for the past two decades, cannot resolve structural variability within tumor subpopulations. Here we identify a subset of cancers that exhibit continuous ultra-low fidelity chromosomal segregation, with single tumors harboring individual cells whose metaphase chromosome counts ranged from 25 to over 200. This remarkable phenotype is recurrent in multiple cancer types and most common in acral melanoma, where it is associated with dicentric chromosomes, translocations, and complex structural variants. Single-cell whole genome sequencing revealed ongoing structural variation and the genomic signature of microhomology-mediated break-induced replication (MMBIR), a backup DNA repair pathway that triggers chromoanasynthesis. These genomes therefore do not pass through isolated catastrophic events and settle into stable lineages but rather undergo continuous evolution of chromosome number and structure across generations, resulting in extreme intratumoral heterogeneity and a shifting repertoire of gene fusions. We anticipate these findings will serve as a starting point for classifying tumors by ongoing karyotypic and structural fluctuation and for testing whether this state confers selective dependence on backup repair pathways.

papers.title: Site-Specific and Diet-Dependent Genetic Architecture of Trabecular Bone in Male BXD Recombinant Inbred Mice
papers.abstract: Vertebral fracture risk is influenced by trabecular bone (Tb) microarchitecture, a phenotype that is regulated by genetic and environmental factors. We examined the genetic architecture of Tb microarchitecture in the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and its modification by dietary calcium (Ca). Male mice from 51 BXD recombinant inbred lines were fed adequate (0.5%) or low (0.25%) Ca diets from 4 to 12 weeks of age. Micro-computed tomography (CT) was used to assess seven L5 Tb phenotypes, and the response to Ca restriction (RCR) was calculated for each phenotype. Quantitative trait loci (QTL) were identified by composite interval mapping and compared with previously reported femoral Tb QTL from the same mice. Genetic background significantly influenced all L5 phenotypes and their responses to Ca restriction. We identified 127 QTL distributed across 61 loci. First, very few L5 QTL overlapped those previously identified in the femur, providing strong evidence for skeletal site-specific genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture. Second, QTL detection was strongly dependent on dietary Ca, with only 4 of 33 loci identified under adequate Ca intake also detected under low Ca intake. Third, QTL controlling the RCR were largely distinct from those controlling L5 phenotypes under either dietary condition. Many loci affected multiple phenotypes, suggesting shared genetic regulation of Tb characteristics. Integration of genetic variation, expression QTL, and existing functional evidence identified plausible candidate genes at several high-priority loci. Together, these findings demonstrate that genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture is both skeletal site-specific and diet-dependent, and that adaptation to dietary Ca restriction has a distinct genetic component.

papers.title: BPEA integrates pleiotropy and epistasis to guide allele pyramiding for multi-trait crop improvement
papers.abstract: Dissecting the genetic basis of complex traits and pyramiding favorable alleles are central to crop breeding. However, jointly evaluating pleiotropy and epistasis to identify allele combinations that meet multiple breeding objectives remains challenging. Here, we present BPEA (Bayesian Pleiotropy and Epistasis Analysis), a Bayesian framework integrating LD-guided QTL interval identification, joint genetic inference and allele-combination assessment. BPEA uses the joint posterior to estimate the posterior probability of simultaneous improvement (PPSI) between allele combinations and ranks them by mean PPSI. In simulations, BPEA improved interval identification and epistatic interaction attribution relative to comparator methods and maintained high precision in shared-signal detection. When epistasis was present, it reduced mean combination-selection regret by 68.4-86.3% relative to a model without interaction terms. Applications to three rapeseed populations identified shared genetic signals and candidate epistatic interactions associated with seed-quality traits. BPEA also prioritized allele combinations for simultaneous reductions in erucic acid and glucosinolate contents and identified complementary parents for cross design. BPEA thus provides a framework for genetic dissection and genomics-guided crop improvement.

papers.title: Quantum-assisted genomic prediction of blast resistance in rice (Oryza sativa L.) using SNP and haplotype representations
papers.abstract: Rice blast caused by Magnaporthe oryzae threatens rice production, and genomic prediction may accelerate identification of resistant germplasm. We evaluated classical machine-learning and simulated quantum-kernel models for binary and three-class prediction of leaf blast (BL) and panicle blast (PB) resistance in 204 rice accessions with 2,120 repeated phenotypic observations. Models used 328,597 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), 104,068 phased haplotypes, or 49,451 unphased haplotypes. Binary prediction outperformed three-class prediction. The highest binary macro-F1 scores were 0.87 for BL and 0.73 for PB. Phased and unphased haplotypes reduced predictor dimensionality by 68.3% and 85.0%, respectively, while retaining broadly comparable performance. Quantum support vector classification achieved competitive results in selected binary tasks but did not consistently exceed the strongest classical models. These findings establish a benchmark for SNP- and haplotype-based prediction of rice blast resistance and for evaluation of quantum machine learning in crop genomics.

papers.title: Systematic prediction of genetic variance in a line development program
papers.abstract: To date, predicting the genetic variance (VG) in biparental crosses has been unreliable. My objective was to determine if predicting VG via tabular analysis, which was developed assuming free recombination and having known VG in founder crosses, is effective even if these unrealistic assumptions are unmet. With line X being developed from the P1/P2 cross, the VG in X/Y was predicted as VX/Y = {lambda}1VP1/Y + {lambda}2VP2/Y, where {lambda}1 was the parental contribution of P1 to X and {lambda}2 was the parental contribution of P2 to X. Simulations involved four founder lines with biallelic marker loci and multiple alleles at quantitative trait loci. The VG in each founder cross was estimated from simulated phenotypic values of N lines under varying heritability (h2). Non-founder lines were developed successively from the founders. Among the 774 non-founder crosses, the mean correlation between the true VG and predicted VG ranged from 0.49 (N = 50 and h2 = 0.20) to 0.70 (N = 400 to 1000 and h2 [≥] 0.50). The mean regression of predicted VG on true VG was 0.51-0.52. Having N = 100-200 lines was sufficient for estimating VG. Free recombination increased the regression of predicted VG on true VG to 0.87 and the correlation between the two to 0.64-0.93. Overall, the results suggested that tabular analysis is currently the most effective method for predicting VG. Further research is needed on combining VG estimates in both founder and non-founder crosses when conducting tabular analysis in a breeding program.

papers.title: Altered age-dependent somatic mutational trajectories in ALS motor cortex neurons
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease in which disease onset is influenced by genetic, age-associated and environmental factors. Somatic mutations accumulate throughout life and may provide a molecular link between aging and neuronal vulnerability. Here, we investigated neuronal somatic mutational patterns in ALS and control motor cortex using three previously generated 10X single-nucleus RNA and ATAC sequencing datasets. Within the genomic regions accessible to 10X sequencing, variant calls showed established features of neuronal somatic mutagenesis, including neuronal enrichment, age-associated accumulation and recovery of the clock-like SBS5 mutational signature. ALS was associated with a disease-specific age-dependent trajectory of neuronal somatic mutation burden, with higher burden in younger ALS donors and a decreasing difference with age. SBS5 represented the largest fitted mutational component and showed a corresponding age-dependent difference. A similar pattern was observed in an independent single-cell whole-genome sequencing dataset. These findings support age-dependent alterations in neuronal somatic mutational patterns in ALS.

papers.title: QuadSeq: A duplicated-duplex DNA-synthesis technology for high-fidelity nanopore sequencing of linear DNA amplicons
papers.abstract: Long-read nanopore sequencing is a highly versatile technology that is currently constrained by high error-rates, which can impair accurate genotyping of complex DNA samples. Common mitigation strategies based on creating consensus sequences from tandem duplications synthesized by rolling-circle or multiple-displacement amplification are prone to create both chimeric DNA molecules and require an initial DNA-circularization. Here we present QuadSeq, a three-step DNA-synthesis technology that can convert linear DNA amplicons into duplicated DNA duplexes that encode two forward and two reverse strand copies of a sequence-of-interest. Intramolecular consensus sequences generated from QuadSeq duplicated DNA duplexes yielded a median single-amplicon accuracy of up to 0.9992 (Q31), without requiring a cumbersome DNA-circularization of the amplicon-of-interest. We can also show that the primary bottleneck for achieving accurate nanopore amplicon sequencing is not the mutation rate of the initial PCR-amplification, but the fidelity of the nanopore sequencing. QuadSeq consensus sequences generated from amplicons synthesized by a low-fidelity DNA polymerase (Taq) had a 6.6-fold lower median error-rate compared to amplicon simplex reads synthesized by a high-fidelity DNA polymerase (Phusion U). Going forward, we predict that the QuadSeq DNA-synthesis technology will enable the use of almost any low-fidelity DNA polymerase for high-fidelity nanopore amplicon sequencing.

papers.title: Single-dose neonatal gene therapy preserves motor coordination and extends survival of Polg-deficient mice
papers.abstract: POLG mutations are the most common single nuclear gene cause of mitochondrial disease. POLG disease spans a spectrum of clinical presentations with variable age of onset and severity. Early-onset disease is often severe and fatal (e.g., Alpers syndrome, myocerebrohepatopathy), while late-onset disease can be relatively mild (e.g., progressive external ophthalmoplegia). POLG disease is incurable, with few symptomatic treatments available, none of which can prevent its progression. Gene replacement therapy has the potential to halt or prevent POLG disease, but its development has been hindered by the large size of the POLG cDNA and the scarcity of suitable mouse models. Here, we developed a bespoke Polg knockout (KO) mouse model by inactivating the Polg locus in parvalbumin-expressing neurons (e.g., Purkinje cells) and fast-twitch skeletal muscle fibers. KO mice developed progressive motor coordination deficits, respiratory chain deficiency in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, and died prematurely. We also developed nine AAV-based gene therapy vectors and confirmed their ability to deliver and express the human POL{gamma}A protein in different mouse tissues. A single high-dose administration of either of two lead candidates into Polg KO neonates preserved respiratory chain activity in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, delayed the onset of motor coordination deficits, and extended lifespan. Thus, our work provides preclinical proof of concept for gene replacement therapy for POLG disease, establishing the feasibility of this approach and laying the foundation for further development in the field.

papers.title: Domain-informed effector gene assignment exposes training-data dependence of drug target prioritisation from GWAS
papers.abstract: About 90% of trait-associated lead variants lie outside protein-coding regions, so nominating the effector gene at genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci remains the principal bottleneck in translating associations into biological insight. Since no experimentally resolved ground truth exists at scale, every method rests on quasi-true-positive sets dominated by a single line of evidence. Here, we benchmarked established prioritisation methods across three independent evaluation sets, trained five models each informed by a different biological domain, and annotated lead variants for six common diseases. Performance did not transfer across domains (AUPRC 0.91 to 0.46 for the same method), and we traced this to how differently models weight the distance between variant and gene (p<5.3x10-123), not to how they were built. Curation assumptions propagated into predictions and can become self-confirming, such as druggability in the Open Targets-informed model. The five models shared only 17.1% to 31.8% of effector gene assignments, converging on established disease biology but diverging where GWAS are expected to yield novel insight. Recovery of 340 approved drug targets differed markedly between models, and no way of combining them, by averaging scores (38.8%) or training on all curations jointly (36.5%), approached the 52.1% recovered across all five together. Our workflow matched Open Targets L2G across three annotation sets without prior biological knowledge and exceeded it where curated knowledge already linked gene and disease. We provide the Domain-informed EFfector gene Assignment framework (DEFA; https://github.com/lkohleick/DEFA), which reports rather than hides the curation assumption behind each gene assignment so that it can be examined and tested.

papers.title: Isolate relatedness is more strongly associated with host and geography compared with phenotypic variation in a broad host range pathogen
papers.abstract: Determining the drivers of diversity in plant pathogen populations is a critical for developing effective management strategies. Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, a cosmopolitan fungus infecting over 400 plant species, causes considerable yield and economic losses worldwide. However, longstanding questions remain about the association between genetic and phenotypic variation in this pathogen, leaving the drivers of its diversification unresolved. Here, we characterized the diversity of S. sclerotiorum isolates from the United States in a global context and tested the hypothesis that phylogenetic relatedness structures phenotypic variation among isolates. Genome-wide variant analysis resolved US isolates into several distinct lineages, with short within-lineage branch lengths consistent with recent common ancestry or clonal propagation. Population structure analysis confirmed two major global clusters, one composed predominantly of Australian isolates and the other largely of isolates from the rest of the world, including the US. Notably, several US isolates grouped within the Australian cluster, suggesting historical intercontinental movement of this pathogen. Contrary to our expectations, isolate relatedness was more strongly associated with data such as host, geographic origin, and year of collection compared with morphological variation, suggesting that phenotypic variation segregates independently of phylogenetic structure. Instead, the distribution of phenotypic variation primarily reflected two trade-offs: rapid radial growth with shorter sclerotial development versus slower growth with prolonged sclerotial development, and the production of many small sclerotia versus fewer larger ones. Together, our results shed light on the complex relationships between phenotypic, ecological, and phylogenetic variation and bring us one step closer to predicting how diversity is structured in natural populations of a global fungal pathogen.

papers.title: A conserved dimerization motif squelches transcription
papers.abstract: Squelching is an indirect inhibition of transcription that results from redistribution of cofactors away from DNA. Here, we describe a class of Lis homology (LisH)-derived peptides that act as transcriptional squelchers. LisH domains are a highly conserved motif found in 10s of thousands of proteins and are composed of ~30 amino acids in a helix-turn-helix fold. By examining a phylogenetically diverse subset of LisH domains in a synthetic Saccharomyces cerevisiae assay, we identified a small number of hydrophobic residues within the first helix that are required for effective inhibition of reporter expression. In addition, squelching required binding to the general transcriptional cofactor Taf5, a subunit of the TFIID complex. Transcriptome-level impacts were largely correlated in yeast expressing two distinct LisH sequences, consistent with a model that LisH-based squelching results from a shared mechanism of sequestering Taf5. Consistent with that inference, overexpression of Taf5 partially reversed the squelching effect. Given the interest in squelching as a potential area for anti-cancer therapies, we also tested whether our shortest squelching sequence called YC5C-H1 had any effect on the human colorectal cancer cell line HCT-15. In addition to preferentially squelching high expression genes, YC5C-H1 sharply slowed growth of HCT-15 cells.

papers.title: Genetic nurture and shared environmental effects across cognitive, educational, and mental health outcomes
papers.abstract: Genetic nurture, in which parental genotype predicts offspring outcomes independent of offspring genotype, operates at the between-family level, corresponding to the shared environmental effect (C) in the classical twin design. Genetic nurture represents a portion of C captured by parental genotype. The link between genetic nurture and C has not been systematically quantified across multiple trait domains. Using 2559 families with genotyped parents and 6710 twin pairs, we estimated genetic nurture using polygenic scores (PGS) and C using the twin design for 40 educational, cognitive, and anthropometric outcomes from age 7 to 26, and for 8 psychopathology symptoms at age 26. Although genetic nurture effects were small, the largest effects were observed for educational outcomes, followed by cognitive abilities, and then psychopathology symptoms. C followed the same pattern. Across eight trait domains, the correlation between genetic nurture and C was 0.68. However, psychopathology outcomes also showed relatively low PGS prediction, which creates a ceiling for estimated genetic nurture. In proportion to PGS prediction, psychopathology showed as much genetic nurture as educational outcomes. Why does psychopathology show genetic nurture despite showing no C? Why is psychopathology PGS prediction so low? We suggest that nonadditive genetic variance could explain both.

papers.title: RNA polymerase II links arsenic exposure to chromosome-wide γH2A signaling
papers.abstract: Arsenic is a widespread environmental carcinogen whose genotoxicity is commonly attributed to oxidative DNA damage and replication-associated lesions. Here, we identify RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) as an important determinant of early arsenic-induced DNA damage checkpoint signaling. In budding yeast, acute As(III) exposure induced rapid, chromosomewide {gamma}H2A accumulation under low oxidative stress, without requiring ongoing bulk DNA replication or causing detectable chromosome fragmentation. Unexpectedly, depletion of Rpb1, the largest subunit of RNAPII and a key component of its catalytic center, markedly attenuated this response. Comparison of different transcriptional perturbations revealed that only selected disruptions of RNAPII function, including Rpb1 inactivation in the rpb1-1 mutant, induced widespread {gamma}H2A accumulation. These contrasting effects suggest that checkpoint activation depends on the presence and particular functional states of RNAPII. Consistent with its involvement, As(III) reduced RNAPII chromatin occupancy and Rpb1 abundance, while arsenic-affinity assays recovered the RNAPII complex. However, As(III) did not measurably inhibit RNA elongation by purified RNAPII in vitro. In human cells, acute As(III) exposure induced ATR phosphorylation and {gamma}H2AX accumulation under low-ROS conditions, while pharmacological inhibition of transcription also triggered {gamma}H2AX phosphorylation. Together, our findings establish an important contribution of RNAPII to early arsenic-induced checkpoint signaling and suggest that the transcription machinery can couple environmental stress to a chromosome-wide DNA damage response.

papers.title: Disruption to rRNA biogenesis triggers histone mRNA 3' misprocessing in C. elegans through genome-surveillance regulators
papers.abstract: Maturation of replication-dependent histone pre-mRNA transcripts involves a 3' cleavage event facilitated by the conserved stem-loop binding protein (SLBP). Cellular conditions that trigger an error in this process are not well understood. Here, we developed a GFP-based in vivo histone 3' misprocessing reporter in Caenorhabditis elegans and performed a genome-wide RNAi screen for histone regulators. We found that depletion of genes involved in various steps of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) biosynthesis triggers misprocessing of histone 3' tail, with the strongest effect observed upon depletion of rpoa-2 encoding the core subunit of RNA polymerase I. Transcriptome sequencing reveals rpoa-2 knockdown mirrors the effect of depleting the C. elegans SLBP homologue CDL-1 at the protein level, indicating that rpoa-2 and CDL-1 co-regulate similar transcriptome targets. Depletion of rpoa-2 impairs endomitosis of the C. elegans intestinal cells and is accompanied by aberrant activation of cell cycle markers in the absence of change in DNA content. Gene interaction analysis shows that rpoa-2 signals through multiple conserved cell cycle regulators, including ATM-1, GEN-1, and LIN-35 to trigger histone misprocessing in both CDL-1 dependent and independent manners. Together, our findings reveal that disruption in the rRNA biogenesis pathway triggers histone misprocessing through conserved genome surveillance pathway regulators.

papers.title: A harmonized functional reference framework for GBA1
papers.abstract: Systematic functional evidence is lacking for most rare GBA1 variants, limiting their interpretation in Gaucher disease (GD) and Parkinsons disease (PD). Here, we used a multiplexed assay of variant effect (MAVE) to generate a comprehensive atlas of lysosome-specific glucocerebrosidase (GCase) activity for more than 10400 GBA1 variants, covering 97 percent of all possible single-amino-acid substitutions. The atlas recapitulated known structural and biochemical determinants of glucocerebrosidase function and revealed concordance between functional impairment and expert-curated pathogenicity classifications. It identified significantly reduced activity in 94 of 186 reported variants of uncertain significance and revealed a quantitative relationship between functional impairment and GD disease severity. Integration with the Global PD Genetics Program associated greater variant-level functional impairment with earlier PD onset and higher PD odds ratios. Independent measurements of lysosomal glucocerebrosidase activity in stable cell lines expressing individual variants validated the MAVE results and resolved subtle functional deficits among variants close to the wild-type range, including established PD risk alleles. These findings provide a functional reference framework linking GBA1 variants to their molecular consequences and clinical phenotypes and demonstrate how comprehensive variant-effect maps can inform genetic interpretation and precision medicine.

papers.title: UV-excited autofluorescence uncovers multicopy suppressors of a Cdc14-associated meiotic defect
papers.abstract: The Cdc14 phosphatase plays essential roles in meiotic chromosome metabolism and cell-cycle progression, yet the cellular pathways capable of compensating for reduced Cdc14 function remain poorly understood. To explore these connections, we performed a multicopy suppressor screen in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, using a mutant CDC14 allele that severely impairs sporulation. UV-excited ascospore-wall autofluorescence enabled the rapid screening of approximately 14,400 transformants, while subsequent microscopy provided quantitative validation of sporulation phenotypes. Photographic image processing facilitated candidate recovery, and a complementary computational analysis of archived images established the reproducibility of fluorescence-associated detections across different acquisition conditions. Genetic screening and independent plasmid retransformation identified four genomic-library plasmids that reproducibly enhanced sporulation. Molecular characterisation of the strongest suppressors revealed genomic regions associated with chromatin regulation and nuclear-pore organisation. Further analysis prioritised two particularly promising candidate genes: RCO1, encoding a component of the Rpd3S histone-deacetylase complex, and POM34, encoding an integral membrane nucleoporin. Suppressor activity was retained in a reduced POM34-containing construct, strengthening its candidacy for further functional investigation. Together, these findings establish an effective fluorescence-guided strategy for multicopy suppressor discovery and reveal promising genetic connections between Cdc14-dependent meiotic progression, chromatin regulation and nuclear architecture.

papers.title: Genome survival and descent in population pedigrees
papers.abstract: Motivated by issues of the maintenance of genetic variation in a highly endangered species, we continue earlier studies into the population genetics ancestry and descent of genome segments. In this paper, we focus on the survival and descent of genome in a population pedigree of a diploid dioecious species. We consider a population potentially being maintained from a small founder base, taking the canonical example a random-mating population of 100 males and 100 females. We show how previous methods to examine the ancestry of a single genome in such a population can also be used to account the survival genetic lengths and number of descendant copies of founder genome segments, and explore the variance of these measures. We show the variance of the population distribution over realizations within a pedigree is scarcely smaller then the variance over pedigrees: variation is in meiosis rather than in pedigree. While all founders continue to lose genome over time, the very first generations are critical to determining the amount of surviving genome. Dependence among founders is slight, except for between the two genomes of a founder: however when monogamy is enforced this high dependence extends to founder mates. We briefly consider extensions of population size (both smaller and larger), of mating structure, and of variance in offspring number, including variance in male reproductive success.

papers.title: LAMP sheds light on how sequence to function models learn variant effects during post-training
papers.abstract: Genomic sequence-to-function (S2F) models show promise for interpreting noncoding genetic variation, yet they currently underestimate the effects of most causal variants. This leads to fine-mapping failures that are reflected in their underperformance relative to linear baselines at predicting gene expression across individuals from personal genome sequences. Improving personal genome predictions, which reflect this underestimation, is therefore critical. There is broad interest in post-training S2F models to improve these predictions, yet many groups have shown that doing so with personal genome sequences and paired expression values does not meaningfully improve predictions on held-out genes and people (HOGP). Why these post-training efforts to improve predictions on HOGP, and therefore causal variant underestimation, remains unclear. To understand why, we introduce LAMP (Learning of Artificial Motif Perturbations), a framework in which artificial SNVs (aSNVs) perturbing transcription factor motifs are substituted into personal genome datasets genome-wide with large, consistent, and causal effects on gene expression. These aSNVs are designed to be deliberately easy to learn, yet fine-tuning Enformer using this LAMP framework led to persistent underperformance on HOGP, which suggests fundamental challenges for learning variant effects during post-training that are independent of the complexity of natural genetic variation. Our findings suggest this underperformance is caused in part due to challenges learning to strengthen enhancer-gene links during post-training. In particular, models struggle with learning to rewire attention weights to relate aSNV detection, over distance, to a change in expression of the target gene. This limitation is caused by strong pre-trained priors that downweight distal regulatory elements, causing extreme data inefficiency in learning to attend to distal elements, and variants within them, during post-training. Second, sequence variability between loci containing different instances of the same TF motif obscures otherwise easy-to-learn motif perturbation patterns and also hinder learning of variant effects. Our results suggest that the scale of observed human genetic variation is vastly insufficient to maximize S2F model accuracy on HOGP via simple fine-tuning, consistent with past outcomes. We propose data augmentation strategies that, under LAMP, significantly improve learning of aSNV effects by strategically targeting the limitations we identified. We release LAMP as a tool to troubleshoot and optimize future S2F post-training objectives.

papers.title: Local GEBVs and additive variance in maize heterotic groups across low- and high-stress environments
papers.abstract: Hybrid maize (Zea mays L.) parents are chosen within heterotic groups. Drought and heat stress are expected to become more frequent, but little is known about how they change the additive variance of each group and where in the genome it lies. We analyzed testcross grain yield from 62 Genomes to Fields environments, classified as low or high stress by climate. For 1,362 parents from three heterotic groups and two doubled-haploid families, we fitted a genomic model with group deviations and calculated local genomic estimated breeding values in 164-kb segments. In the heterotic groups, high stress reduced additive variance by 4057%, and the genetic correlation between conditions was 0.730.99. Within groups, the distribution of variance across the genome was similar between conditions (correlation 0.841.00), and genotype-by-environment interaction was spread over many low-variance segments. Genome-wide association detected 25 loci under low stress and 18 under high stress, none shared, but half or more lay in high-effect, high-variance segments that were nearly the same in both conditions. The best possible cross between the two heterotic pools exceeded the best evaluated hybrid by 105117%, a gap that depended on segment size, not on stress. With 25 founders, stacking the best segments reached 9495% of the pool potential, versus 5692% for selection on total breeding value, whose founders were more related. Founders chosen in one condition reached, in the other, 94100% of the potential of those chosen there. Local breeding values can guide the choice of donors and founders under both conditions.

papers.title: Sequential co-translational assembly of the yeast SAGA DUB module precedes post-translational core docking.
papers.abstract: The 1.8-megadalton SAGA coactivator is organized into discrete functional modules, yet how individual catalytic modules are assembled and integrated into the holo-complex remains poorly understood. Here, we dissect the assembly pathway of the four-subunit histone H2B deubiquitinating (DUB) module in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Pairwise RIP-qPCR uncovers a unidirectional network of co-translational interactions sequentially linking Sus1, Sgf11, Ubp8, and Sgf73. Combining systematic deletion genetics with co-immunoprecipitation and quantitative NanoBiT assays in intact living cells, we demonstrate that these contacts form an obligate linear cascade rather than independent binary events: each upstream subcomplex licenses the next nascent-chain engagement, sustains downstream Sgf11 and Ubp8 stability, and precludes post-translational bypass. Conversely, DUB subunits exhibit no co-translational interactions with the SAGA core interface, indicating that completed modules dock post-translationally. Thus, unlike single-scaffold assembly models, SAGA separates multi-step co-translational module templating from post-translational holo-complex docking, safeguarding compositional fidelity.

papers.title: A single kindred across centuries: patrilineal continuity and a female-mediated increase in the local genetic component of the Lake Onega area at the Kondopoga cemetery
papers.abstract: We report the first genome-wide ancient DNA data from a medieval population in the territory of the modern Republic of Karelia, Russia: 1240K capture data for 22 individuals from the Kondopoga cemetery on Lake Onega, a churchyard used from the 12th to the 19th century. Combining relatedness estimates, autosomal and X-chromosomal identity-by-descent, uniparental lineages, burial position and archaeological dating, we place eight individuals in a single pedigree spanning five generations, anchored on a founding couple buried in the highest part of the cemetery. Identity-by-descent links almost all the remaining individuals to that couple, indicating that the sample is not a cross-section of a local population but a single kindred, which is the object of this study. Within it, the founding males paternal lineage recurs from the 12th-13th to the 16th century, mitochondrial lineages differ between individuals of the same generation, and autosomal ancestry shifts between generations rather than between archaeological phases. The ancestry of the founders is closest to populations from northwestern Rus and the eastern Baltic, while the Uralic-related ancestry entering the pedigree is best modelled using present-day Finnic groups of the region. The family was patrilineal, and its profile was reshaped by the women who married into it.

papers.title: TEV Induced Cleavage of Nuclei Tagged in Specific Cell Types (TIC-TaC) reveals histone profiles of activated neurons
papers.abstract: Epigenomic profiling methods such as CUT&RUN/Tag are commonly employed to evaluate the genomic localization of histone modifications, transcription factors, and chromatin regulating proteins. Numerous transgenic mouse models also exist that label specific cell populations by leveraging Cre-based recombination and fluorescent reporters to allow for cell type specific epigenetic profiling in vivo. However, none of these systems allow for rapid, parallel processing for cell-type-specific CUT&RUN/Tag. Here, we report the development of TEV Induced Cleavage of Nuclei Tagged in Specific Cell Types (TIC-TaC) in which we leverage a recombination-based system that results in conditional expression of a Sun1-GFP fusion protein with a TEV site introduced between Sun1 and GFP. Like the existing INTACT system, nuclei tagged by cell-type specific Cre recombinase activity can be efficiently purified using immunoprecipitation to allow for rapid, efficient, and in parallel nuclei isolation. However, with the addition of TEV protease, TIC-TaC nuclei can be subsequently removed from the beads allowing for downstream CUT&RUN/Tag. We applied this system to neurons isolated from the cortex to define the effects of seizure induced neuronal activation on numerous histone modifications and histone variant proteins and identified concordant shifts in H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H2A.Z and H2BE at seizure responsive genes. Together, through the development and application of TIC-TaC to allow for parallel processing of tissue for cell-type specific analysis, we uncover activity-dependent regulation of chromatin in the brain.

papers.title: The program STRUCTURE is good at detecting contemporary hybridization
papers.abstract: The program STRUCTURE is widely used in conservation genetics to detect human-caused hybridization between previously isolated populations. However, its performance at this specific task is not yet known, and methods used to interpret the model output vary widely among studies. We simulated hybridization between two populations on the timescale of real-world cases and tested STRUCTURE's ability to correctly detect hybridization based on a simple "hybrid signal": inferring the presence or absence of a minimum of one hybrid. Overall, this returned the correct result in 100% of scenarios when Fst between the two populations was between 0.05-0.15 when using an optimal Q-threshold of 0.10. Performance was slightly reduced when divergence was very weak (Fst = 0.01, with an optimal Q-threshold between 0.30-0.35) or when the population receiving migrants was substructured, but it still returned the correct result in 89-100% of cases, depending on simulation parameters. We conclude that STRUCTURE, paired with this hybrid signal and our recommended Q-thresholds, is an appropriate tool for detecting contemporary hybridization.

papers.title: sHSP-induced oligomerization enhances mammalian transcription factor potency
papers.abstract: Recently, a non-canonical role for small heat shock proteins (sHSPs) was identified, wherein sHSP-induced oligomerization drives targeted genomic accumulation of an endogenous silencing complex. Here we repurpose this property to develop sHSPs as compact, tunable tags for transcriptional engineering. Screening sHSPs across the tree of life, we show that sHSPs fused to transcription factors (TFs) can increase on-target genomic occupancy, recruit sHSP-tagged proteins, and amplify target-gene activation in mammalian cells. Distinct sHSPs vary in levels of transcriptional occupancy and output, providing a means to tune TFs activity while maintaining targeting specificity. This work establishes sHSPs as a new class of compact (~20kDa), tunable, activity-enhancing tags with broad potential for transcriptional engineering and synthetic biology.

papers.title: Sequencing of the Prnp-Prnd deletion junction in Prn-/- mouse tissues after formaldehyde fixation and >22 years at room temperature.
papers.abstract: In 2004, Nicolas Genoud and colleagues reported that deletion of Prnd, which encodes Doppel, prevented neurodegeneration in mice with extensive Prnp deletions. The work tested the proposal that abnormal Doppel expression in the brain caused cerebellar degeneration in mice lacking the cellular prion protein, PrP. Advances in automated image analysis have expanded scrutiny of published figures, and post-publication reviews have raised concerns about apparent figure manipulation in this work, calling its authenticity and reliability into question. Here we assemble the surviving contemporaneous records of the original work and report new experiments on archived tissue. To reassess the reported genetic rearrangement, DNA from archived paraffin-embedded brain tissue was amplified across the putative deletion junction and analyzed by bidirectional Sanger sequencing and comparison with mouse reference sequences. The two reads spanned 607 positions and placed Prnp-side sequence, a 34-base loxP site and Prnd-side sequence in the expected order, with 93 intervening bases that matched bacteriophage P1 loxP-flanking and plasmid cloning-site sequences rather than the mouse reference and therefore probably derive from the targeting construct. Independent de novo reassembly from the 2025 Sanger chromatogram files reproduced the junction sequence; the assemblies differed only at three terminal bases with low base-call quality. These findings support the expected local junction arrangement and provide a publicly inspectable sequence description that extends the molecular information presented in the original paper. The amplicon size and the position of the loxP site match the values stated in the original paper, as does the approximately 18-kb distance between the two flanking sequences in the wild-type genome, which the deletion brings together. Recovery of junction DNA after more than two decades of room-temperature storage as paraformaldehyde-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue demonstrates the value of retained material for reassessing historical experimental claims.

papers.title: Population-aware computational assessment of base-editing accessibility among pathogenic variants on human chromosome 21: an African-ancestry-focused pilot study
papers.abstract: Background Population-aware gene-editing research requires independent evaluation of clinical variant evidence, ancestry-stratified allele observations, nucleotide correction chemistry, and sequence-level editing constraints. We developed a source-traceable chromosome 21 pilot connecting these dimensions without equating computational accessibility with therapeutic editability. Methods Reviewed ClinVar pathogenic/likely pathogenic single-nucleotide variants were matched by GRCh38 chromosome, position, REF and ALT to overall and African/African-American (AFR) gnomAD v4.1 exome allele counts. Exploratory frequency contrasts used two-sided Fisher exact tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Higher-confidence variants with canonical adenine or cytosine base-editing chemistry underwent NGG PAM/editor-window screening, bystander enumeration, MANE v1.5 consequence annotation, theoretical joint-product assessment and chromosome 21-restricted guide-homology searches. Results Among 1,944 ClinVar variants, 851 matched gnomAD; 694 were quality-filtered and alternate-allele-observed overall, including 300 higher-confidence records. Six variants met exploratory AFR-elevation criteria. Of 234 higher-confidence ABE/CBE chemistry-compatible variants, 118 (50.4%) had at least one nominal NGG/PAM-window placement, 55 (23.5%) a nominal zero-bystander placement, and 44 (18.8%) a zero-bystander placement without an additional chromosome 21 NGG near-match within three mismatches. The 261 placements generated 295 hypothetical bystander events (195 distinct alleles); five distinct potential products overlapped pathogenic/likely pathogenic ClinVar alleles. Across placements, 764 theoretical target-corrected sequence states were enumerated, of which 503 contained at least one bystander. Three variant-level editing-accessibility comparisons between AFR-observed and AFR-unobserved alleles were not statistically significant (BH q=1.0). Conclusions Canonical correction chemistry substantially overestimates nominal local base-editor accessibility. A population-aware, transcript-informed computational framework can identify hypotheses for follow-up, but allele-frequency contrasts, guide-similarity results and enumerated sequence products do not establish clinical efficacy, experimental editing specificity or genome-wide off-target safety.

papers.title: Language-Driven Clustering of Transfer, Persistence, Prevalence & Recovery Studies for Forensic Activity-Level Evaluation
papers.abstract: Transfer, Persistence, Prevalence, and Recovery (TPPR) data are essential for forensic activity level evaluations (ALE); however, concerns remain regarding the accessibility of relevant literature. This study investigated whether automated literature retrieval and natural language processing (NLP) methods could be used to identify and characterize TPPR studies. Existing forensic repositories were combined with records retrieved through the Web of Science Application Programming Interface (API) and enriched with bibliographic metadata, producing a corpus of 3,279 unique records. Automated retrieval tools were evaluated, and transformer-based topic modeling was applied to examine the breadth of the literature. The results showed that database APIs provided the most reliable mechanism for literature retrieval, while topic modeling identified meaningful groupings corresponding to major forensic disciplines and trace evidence types. The findings indicate that TPPR literature exists and that automated methods can support its discovery and organization. Although the availability of literature does not necessarily imply suitability for ALE, the results suggest that the principal challenge is the discovery, assessment, and reuse of published studies rather than their absence. Automated retrieval, semantic search, and quality assessment frameworks may improve access to relevant evidence and support the development of forensic knowledge systems for evaluative reporting and Bayesian network construction.

papers.title: Unravelling the hidden diversity of the monkfish Lophius gastrophysus using integrative taxonomy
papers.abstract: The monkfish Lophius gastrophysus is a commercially exploited demersal species distributed along the continental shelf and slope of the western Atlantic Ocean. Like other anglerfish species, L. gastrophysus has a pelagic larval stage that can facilitate dispersal by oceanic currents (Farina et al., 2008). It is considered the most widely distributed species in the genus, spanning more than 10,000 km of the western Atlantic Coast, from North Carolina to Argentina. Previous morphological analyses based on a limited set of traits suggested that L. gastrophysus may comprise two distinct species. We tested this hypothesis by combining molecular and morphometric data. Sequence data were obtained from 38 L. gastrophysus individuals collected from Northern and Southern American populations. We also used a subset of 13 specimens for geometric morphometrics. Phylogenetic analyses and automatic species delimitation methods consistently distinguished Northern and Southern Atlantic L. gastrophysus as separate clades, and geometric morphometrics supported the same split. The congruence among geographic, molecular, and morphometric data indicates that L. gastrophysus harbours two distinct lineages, highlighting the need for a formal taxonomic revision and separate fisheries management of northern and southern Atlantic populations.

papers.title: Is the Bitter Lesson coming to genomic prediction? An untuned tabular foundation model matches or beats specialized methods
papers.abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) is dominated by models designed around assumptions about how genetic variation affects phenotypes. Here we asked how well a general-purpose pretrained tabular foundation model called TabPFN-3.5 does with no genetics-specific modeling and no tuning when given marker genotypes directly. We benchmarked TabPFN-3.5 using a published comparison of 18 GP methods on 18 traits in six plant species. Against the published means, TabPFN-3.5 ranked first on 11 of 18 traits and had the best median rank. Because the published benchmark did not identify its test sets, we reran GBLUP, RKHS and elastic-net models on the same splits as TabPFN-3.5. Against the best of these, TabPFN-3.5 was significantly behind on only one trait, spruce wood density, and ahead on 12 of 18, with significant gains on all three soybean traits and rice flowering time. In the soybean panel, which had the largest number of lines, its advantage was clearest. In leave-families-out cross-validation, where models were trained on some soybean families and used to predict lines from other families withheld from training, every model lost accuracy and TabPFN-3.5 performed on par with GBLUP and RKHS. That a general-purpose learner matches or exceeds decades of specialized GP models is consistent with Sutton's Bitter Lesson, which holds that methods that scale with computation eventually overtake those built on human knowledge of the domain.
